description: Ninth Vanguard uses AI to spot hidden objects moving in NASA’s SPHEREx sky scans. Led by award-winning AI developer Aarav, we are building an interactive map to hunt for Planet X.
summary: Perturbation is a website for exploring NASA SPHEREx infrared images and watching the sky change. SPHEREx maps the whole sky in 102 infrared colours and returns to each patch about every six months, but its images are large and technical. Perturbation lets anyone pick a patch of sky, blink between visits as Clyde Tombaugh did to find Pluto, subtract them into difference images and read spectra; for the challenge's five stars it also measures motion and brightness. Two small neural networks trained on SPHEREx data help: one flags moving and changing objects with a calibrated confidence and a stated false-alarm rate, the other suggests what kind of object a spectrum belongs to, and an AI page shows exactly what they see and decide. Tested on the challenge's five stars, it measures Barnard's Star moving 10.55 ± 0.12 arcseconds a year (Gaia DR3 for 2026: 10.41), and it finds Pluto, the first Planet X, in 236 SPHEREx images, its sharpest positions a median 0.2 arcseconds from where JPL predicts. Every number names its source.
details:
What it does

Perturbation is a website for exploring NASA SPHEREx infrared images and seeing what changes between visits. The Sky is a 3D globe of the SPHEREx all-sky map with 117,955 clickable Hipparcos stars; in 3D space, stars within about 3,000 light-years move out to their distances from the Sun, on a log scale, and clicking one dims the rest so it stands out. The Lab is a workbench for any patch of sky: blink between visits, as Clyde Tombaugh did to find Pluto; view difference images; lay WISE images from about 2010 over SPHEREx today; and read the 102-band spectrum of any star. For the five challenge stars it also blinks WISE against SPHEREx, shows the measured motion and brightness, and exports the measurements as CSV. Its side panels can be hidden, as in a code editor, so the image gets the whole screen. The AI page shows what the two neural networks see and decide, with every candidate the automatic search found and a live spectral classifier to try. The Planet X page follows Pluto, the first Planet X, through SPHEREx's images. Guided tours with a demonstration pointer teach the Sky globe and the Lab step by step.

How it works

Data. The Python backend finds SPHEREx images through IRSA's image search (Data Release 1 and Quick Release 3) and reads only the bytes it needs: 0.5 to 0.8 MB of each 65 MB file, with pixels identical to IRSA's cutouts.

Pipeline. Each visit's exposures are stacked per detector, with zodiacal light subtracted and flagged pixels left out; differences are divided by their measured noise. Star fits in every exposure give positions; a straight line through them, after removing parallax, gives the proper motion. Spectra come from single exposures or the DR1 spectral cube.

Models. A small convolutional network (43,812 weights) calls each change a mover, variable, artifact or nothing. Trained on synthetic sources planted in real SPHEREx images of 31 fields, it classes 83.7% of stamps correctly on 9 others. A second network (143,431 weights) names one of seven kinds of object from a spectrum, matching the catalogue class for 76% of 5,647 spectra in held-out sky tiles.

Statistics. Scores become conformal p-values against 3,400 scores from separate validation fields; Benjamini-Hochberg q-values within each field decide what is reported. At q ≤ 0.05, on average at most 1 in 20 reported candidates should be false.

What it found

On the challenge's five stars, Epsilon Indi B moves 4.699 ± 0.016 arcseconds a year in SPHEREx images (Gaia DR3, moved to 2026: 4.685). Barnard's Star moves 10.55 ± 0.12 (Gaia: 10.41), 6 degrees off in direction because its positions in one visit are biased. WISE 0855−0714 shifts 7.98 ± 0.77 arcseconds in a year (predicted: 8.04), RW Aurigae faded by 0.86 ± 0.04 magnitudes, and R Draconis's pulsation is recovered. At known positions, the automatic finder recovers Epsilon Indi B and WISE 0855−0714. Across 53 survey fields (1.47 square degrees) it reports two candidates at q ≤ 0.05, both known ultracool dwarfs in training fields: SSSPM J1444−2019, moving 3.66 ± 0.43 arcseconds a year (catalogue: 3.51), and a possible brightening of 2MASS J13243553+6358281 that forced photometry does not confirm. Held-out fields gave no false alarms (at most 12.2 per square degree, 95% upper limit). No new object is claimed.

Pluto, the first Planet X, lands on a detector in 236 SPHEREx images (118 exposures in four visits, April 2025 to October 2026). In its 59 sharpest measurements (S/N 20 or more), its positions differ from JPL Horizons' prediction by 0.18 and 0.20 arcseconds rms (east, north), 90% within 0.41 arcseconds; its spectrum shows methane-ice bands 31%, 62% and 89% deep; and stacking 17 faint frames along its predicted path raises its signal-to-noise from 2.5 in a single frame to 7.3. A Planet Nine as predicted would be 14 to 21 times fainter than SPHEREx's four-survey depth at 3.4 µm, so SPHEREx could not find one, and the site says so.

Benefits and intended impact

The site already uses SPHEREx Data Release 1, released in November 2026. Students, teachers and amateur astronomers can watch a star move without downloading anything; scientists get the measurements, uncertainties and validation reports. The code is open source (Apache-2.0).

What makes it creative

It brings the blink comparator to a 102-colour infrared survey, and it shows its AI openly: the exact cutouts a network looked at, how sure it is, and a false-alarm rate in plain words instead of a bare score. Reading about 1% of each file lets the Lab build any patch of sky live. Every number says where it comes from, and the limits are stated as plainly as the results.

What we considered

- Saturation: Barnard's Star is saturated in 357 of 358 exposures, RW Aurigae in 306 of 335, R Draconis in all 842; the automatic finder misses them and the spectral classifier declines them. The hand measurements above use single exposures and keep saturated pixels whose first reads still give a valid slope (R Draconis: a ring 8 to 12 pixels out). Saturated photometry of the steady Barnard's Star still varies by 0.2 to 0.6 magnitudes between visits, so only larger changes, like RW Aurigae's fade, count; its ± 0.04 is statistical only.

- Sub-pixel motion: with 6.15-arcsecond pixels and visits spanning about a year, a star moving 1 arcsecond a year shifts a sixth of a pixel. Of synthetic movers at S/N 10 or more, 71% that shift a pixel or more are reported, but only 1% of those under a quarter pixel.

- False discoveries: residuals of bright static stars are removed; 3 of 540 synthetic steady stars were reported.

- Archive outages: CDS Strasbourg has been degraded since about 9 November, so SIMBAD and VizieR go through mirrors; IRSA calls are retried and cached, and when IRSA's image search failed on 15 November the Pluto search read the SPHEREx copy in the cloud instead.

- Honest errors: the spectral classifier gets two challenge targets wrong (both brown dwarfs, a class with only 64 training spectra); the Lab shows the catalogue class beside its answer.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

Python 3.13, TypeScript, JavaScript, GLSL and CSS. Website: Next.js 16, React 19, three.js with React Three Fiber, Aladin Lite, Recharts, Tailwind CSS. Backend: FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, photutils, reproject. Training: PyTorch 2.15, scikit-learn. Tests: pytest, Playwright (Chrome, Safari's WebKit and Firefox), axe-core. Hosting: Vercel (website and API). Hardware: one Windows 11 computer, CPU only, no GPU.
